checked_sources: Murakami & Okada 2006 (abstract via Europe PMC REST; full text not accessible: PMC CAPTCHA, Wiley client error)
Galloni et al. 2020 (full text XML, Europe PMC PMC7334021)
Markram et al. 1997 (abstract via Europe PMC REST; full text not in PMC)
evidence_location: Murakami abstract (envelope -0.41 to -0.90 pA m); Galloni Results/Fig. 3-4 legends (apical trunk 600 vs 200 um reduced models; main bifurcation 620 vs 370 um from soma); Markram abstract item 7 (quantal conductance)
quote: The inferred quantal peak conductance increase varied between 1.5 and 5.5 nS (mean, 3 nS).
discrepancy: Arithmetic (0.5 pA m / 0.5 mm = 1 nA) is correct and the inputs are order-of-magnitude consistent, but: (1) Markram 1997 nowhere states '~100 pA per synapse'; its abstract gives a quantal peak conductance of 1.5-5.5 nS (mean 3 nS) at -60 mV, which implies roughly 90-330 pA per contact (mean ~180 pA) only after assuming a ~60 mV driving force; (2) Murakami's envelope is -0.41 to -0.90 pA m, so 0.5 pA m sits at the low end (range implies 0.8-1.8 nA), and the envelope arises from a somatically stimulated intracellular burst discharge, not a 'synaptic burst'; (3) Galloni gives mouse L5 apical trunk lengths (~370-620 um to the main bifurcation) but never discusses sink-source separation; 0.5 mm is the website's own rounding.
suggested_fix: Say the 1 nA is an order-of-magnitude estimate: 'dipole moment ~0.4-0.9 pA m (Murakami & Okada 2006, burst envelope) over an apical trunk of ~0.4-0.6 mm (Galloni et al. 2020) gives ~1-2 nA; for comparison a single synaptic contact with a quantal conductance of 1.5-5.5 nS (Markram et al. 1997) passes on the order of 100-300 pA.'
bibliographic_issues: None found (J Physiol 575(Pt 3):925-936; eLife 9:e55761; J Physiol 500(Pt 2):409-440 all match Europe PMC).

checked_sources: Murakami & Okada 2006 (abstract via Europe PMC REST; full text inaccessible)
quote: The envelope was similar in magnitude (-0.41 to -0.90 pA m) across the four layer V pyramidal cells.
discrepancy: All numbers match (L5 spikes -0.78 to 2.97 pA m, n = 4; L5 envelope -0.41 to -0.90; L2/3 spike 0.47 and envelope -0.29 pA m). Minor nuance: the envelope values are negative in the source (current directed away from the pia, opposite to most spikes), and the claim quotes them unsigned while giving signs for the spikes.
suggested_fix: Optionally: 'envelope -0.41 to -0.90 pA m (i.e. 0.41-0.90 pA m directed away from the pia)' and 'L2/3: envelope -0.29 pA m, spike +0.47 pA m'.
bibliographic_issues: None (J Physiol 575(Pt 3):925-936, DOI resolves in Europe PMC).

checked_sources: Hämäläinen et al. 1993 (full PDF from Aalto repository acris.aalto.fi, RevModPhys.65.413.pdf)
Murakami & Okada 2006 (abstract via Europe PMC REST)
evidence_location: Hämäläinen Sec. I.B (The human brain) and Sec. II.C (Postsynaptic potentials); Murakami abstract, final sentence
quote: strength of a dipole, caused by the synchronous activity of probably tens of thousands of neurons, is 10 nA m
discrepancy: None of substance. Hämäläinen hedges ('probably tens of thousands') and the 10 nAm statements refer to dipoles explaining measured magnetic fields (MEG); 'routinely measured' paraphrases the source's 'typical' / 'Usually ... on the order of 10 nAm'. Hämäläinen also adds 'about a million synapses must be simultaneously active'. Murakami: 'may be detectable with MEG and EEG when 10 000-50 000 cells are synchronously active.'
bibliographic_issues: None (Rev Mod Phys 65(2):413-497 confirmed on the PDF).

checked_sources: Buzsáki, Anastassiou & Koch 2012 (NIH author-manuscript PDF mirrored at bio.fsu.edu; Europe PMC XML returned HTTP 500)
Teleńczuk et al. 2017 (full text XML, Europe PMC PMC5225490)
evidence_location: Buzsáki: section 'Synaptic activity' (p. 2-3 of manuscript, refs 26-30, Fig. 2b,c); Teleńczuk: Results (Fig. 3D-F) and Discussion
quote: in actively spiking neurons the membrane is depolarized, and therefore inhibitory (and often hyperpolarizing) currents can generate substantial transmembrane currents
discrepancy: Minor condition dropped: Buzsáki says GABA-A currents are 'typically assumed to add very little' and that they 'can generate substantial transmembrane currents' specifically when the membrane is depolarized in actively spiking neurons; the claim states it unconditionally. Teleńczuk part is supported: inhibitory dominance is inferred from latency (FS-triggered wst-LFP peaks before RS) and identical polarity; 'both the RS and FS neurons produced negative-going wst-LFPs of similar amplitudes' and st-LFP amplitudes at 0.4-2 mm showed no significant differences 'except the second night of the first human subject' (where inhibitory wst-LFPs were larger, Suppl. Fig. 7B). In monkey premotor cortex the latency difference was not significant.
suggested_fix: 'Inhibitory (GABA-A) currents, often assumed negligible, can generate substantial transmembrane currents when the membrane is depolarized in actively spiking neurons (Buzsáki et al. 2012); ... (inferred from timing and polarity; amplitudes of inhibitory and excitatory unitary fields were similar, with one recording as exception).'
bibliographic_issues: None (Nat Rev Neurosci 13(6):407-420; Sci Rep 7:40211 both confirmed).

checked_sources: Ramon et al. 2014 (full text XML, Europe PMC PMC4122221)
McCann, Pisano & Beltrachini 2019 (full text XML, Europe PMC PMC6708046)
evidence_location: Ramon: Introduction (0.04x CSF), Methods (0.02-0.1 S/m, midrange 0.06 S/m), Table 1 (Dura 1,667 (1,000-5,000) ohm cm = 6E-4 S/cm), Abstract (about 20%), Results/Fig. 3 (40%); McCann: Results text and Table (Dura: single value 0.461 S/m, 1 paper)
quote: range from 0.02 to 0.1 S/m (Oozeer et al., 2005). For our work, we used a midrange value of 0.06
discrepancy: All numbers found. Ramon: 'The conductivity of the dura layer is approximately 0.04 times the conductivity of the CSF'; 'scalp potentials decrease by about 20%'; at the peak location 12.5 uV -> 7.5 uV, 'reduced the amplitude of the scalp potential by 40%'. McCann: 'Insufficient data was available to calculate regression statistics for muscle, fat, blood, the epileptogenic zone, the dura layer and the cerebellum.' Two nuances not in the claim: McCann's sole tabulated dura value is 0.461 S/m (about 8x Ramon's 0.06 S/m); and Ramon's own abstract misstates the values ('conductivities of dura and CSF were 0.001 S/m and 0.06 S/m'), inconsistent with its Methods/Table 1 (0.06 and 1.54 S/m) - the website follows the Methods/Table values, which is correct.
suggested_fix: Optionally add: 'the only value McCann et al. tabulate for dura is 0.461 S/m from a single study'.

checked_sources: Nunez, Nunez & Srinivasan 2019 (bioRxiv v2 full text 10.1101/391318 via WebFetch; Springer page abstract/references only)
de Munck & Peters 1993 (abstract via Europe PMC REST)
Zhang 1995 (abstract via Europe PMC REST)
Berg & Scherg 1994 (abstract via Europe PMC REST)
evidence_location: Nunez Sec. 6.4 (Modeling scalp potential magnitudes with head models); the three method papers' abstracts
quote: Berg and Scherg's fast computation method is extended to multilayer anisotropic spheres.
discrepancy: Zhang (1995) is mischaracterised: its abstract describes it as an extension of Berg & Scherg's fast approximation (fitting 'Berg parameters') to multilayer anisotropic spheres, not an exact series solution. de Munck & Peters 1993 is correctly an exact series expansion ('A series expansion is derived for the potential distribution, caused by a dipole source in a multilayered sphere with piecewise constant conductivity', with addition-subtraction acceleration); Berg & Scherg 1994 is correctly a fast approximation ('3 suitably located dipoles in a homogeneous sphere ... more than 30-fold increase in computing speed'). Radii supported: Nunez 'In our simulations, sphere radii are (brain, CSF, skull, scalp) = (8.0, 8.1, 8.6, 9.2 cm)' and 'The standard head model employed here consists of four concentric spherical shells' - but Nunez also calls it 'only a very approximate head model'; 'the standard analytic EEG forward model' is the website's framing, not Nunez's wording. Nunez's reference list does not cite de Munck, Zhang or Berg & Scherg.
suggested_fix: '...exact series solutions for multilayer (isotropic) spheres are given by de Munck & Peters (1993); Berg & Scherg (1994) give a fast three-dipole approximation, which Zhang (1995) extended to multilayer anisotropic spheres.' Consider 'a standard' rather than 'the standard analytic'.
bibliographic_issues: None: Brain Topogr 32(2):193-214; IEEE TBME 40(11):1166-1174; Phys Med Biol 40(3):335-349; EEG Clin Neurophysiol 90(1):58-64 all match Europe PMC. Could not verify Zhang's full text, so whether it also reproduces the exact anisotropic series is unconfirmed.

checked_sources: Ronca et al. 2024 (full text XML, Europe PMC PMC11505294)
evidence_location: Introduction (blink rate, 3-15 Hz bandwidth); Sec. 3 regression-method description (15 Hz, Fig. 3); Sec. 3 formula (2) discussion (frontal electrodes); Fig. 1 legend
quote: occurrences ranging from 12 to 18 blinks per minute
discrepancy: None. Also: 'the main spectral content of ocular blinks is up to 15 Hz (Figure 3)'; 'their bandwidth (3-15 Hz) overlaps with ... theta and alpha bands'; 'electrodes closer to the eye location, such as the frontal ones, will be more affected'. checked_sources: Boudewyn et al. 2018 (abstract only, via Europe PMC REST). Full text attempts failed: Wiley full/pdf (client error/403), PMC5940511 (CAPTCHA), Europe PMC fullTextXML (HTTP 500) and render PDF (403), eScholarship qt5qk50168 PDF (HTTP 202, empty body), CORE API (429). The UC Davis/owlstown PDFs found by search were a different 2023 paper (psyp.14363).
quote: Each of these issues was examined in the context of the error-related negativity and the lateralized readiness potential.
discrepancy: Could not verify. The abstract confirms the paper concerns ERN and LRP and 'the noise level', but contains no sqrt(N) statement, no amplitude ranges (5-15 uV ERN, 1-4 uV LRP) and no statement that single-trial noise is much larger than the signal. The sqrt(N) rule is textbook signal averaging and the amplitude ranges are plausible, but neither was seen in this source.
suggested_fix: Verify against the full text (Introduction) or cite a textbook (e.g. Luck, An Introduction to the ERP Technique) for sqrt(N) and the component amplitudes.

checked_sources: Chi, Jung & Cauwenberghs 2010 (full PDF from isn.ucsd.edu/pub/papers/rbme10.pdf)
Chi, Maier & Cauwenberghs 2011 (abstract via OpenAlex; IEEE Xplore page returned nothing)
Taheri, Knight & Smith 1994 (abstract via Europe PMC REST; full text not accessible)
evidence_location: Chi 2010 Sec. II (Electrode model, Fig. 2: LMP7702 with 5 pF input capacitance; active shielding), Sec. III.B/C (insulated: '300 pF [26] to several nanofarads'; noncontact: '10's pF'); Chi 2011 abstract; Chi 2010 reference list ([9] = Taheri 1994, [26] = Alizadeh-Taheri 1996)
quote: the coupling capacitance for insulated electrodes is relatively large, from 300 pF [26] to several nanofarads
discrepancy: All numbers are in the sources, but the ~300 pF figure is misattributed: Chi 2010 cites it to its reference [26] = B. Alizadeh-Taheri, R. L. Smith, R. T. Knight, 'An active, microfabricated, scalp electrode array for EEG recording', Sensors and Actuators A 54(1-3):606-611, 1996 - not to Taheri et al. 1994 (Chi's [9]), which is cited only for the original insulated-electrode design. Taheri 1994's abstract gives a 3 mm steel disk with a 200 nm nitride coating (which implies ~2 nF) but I could not see a stated capacitance. Nuance dropped: Chi 2010 says noncontact electrodes 'have been typically described simply as coupling signals through a small capacitance (10's pF)' but 'In reality, however, there is typically an important' resistive component as well. Chi 2011 abstract supports exactly: 'input impedance of 60 fF || 50 TOhm' and 'electrode coupling capacitances as low as 0.5 pF'; Chi 2010: 'unity gain connected LMP7702 with 5 pF input capacitance' plus active-shield discussion.
suggested_fix: Cite the 300 pF figure to Alizadeh-Taheri, Smith & Knight (1996) Sens. Actuators A 54:606-611 (via Chi et al. 2010), or drop the Taheri 1994 citation for that number; consider 'nominally tens of picofarads (with a non-negligible resistive component in practice)'.
bibliographic_issues: Chi 2011: IEEE JETCAS 1(4):526-535 confirmed via OpenAlex (not indexed in PubMed/Europe PMC). Others match.

checked_sources: Iivanainen et al. 2021 (full text XML, Europe PMC PMC8752968); arXiv 1912.05401 metadata via arXiv API
evidence_location: Abstract; Sec. 3.2 Results (B99% percentiles and sensor spacings); Sec. 4.1 Discussion (~120 sensors); Appendix C / Fig. C.11 (head-model comparison)
quote: the 1S model produces essentially larger numbers, the median reaching 291 (vs. 80 in the 4C model)
discrepancy: Supported: 'approximately 280, 90 and 110 SF components were needed in on-scalp, off-scalp MEG and EEG'; most superficial bin 97.5th percentiles 276/93/109 with 'corresponding uniform sensor spacings 1.6, 3.3 and 2.6 cm'; 'the sensor count should be at least roughly 120'. Differences: (1) on-scalp MEG is ~280 (276) in the analysis; 'roughly 300' appears only in the Conclusions; (2) 'without a skull the count rises to 300-350' is not stated - the text gives a median of 291 (vs 80 for the 4C model) and the model is a homogeneous single-shell (1S) conductor bounded by the scalp, i.e. no skull AND no CSF; the claim also compares the 4C 97.5th-percentile (110) with what is at best a 1S median/percentile mix; 300-350 may be read off Fig. C.11 but is not in the text.
suggested_fix: '...without the skull/CSF layers (a homogeneous single-shell model) the median count for the most superficial sources rises from 80 to about 290' and 'versus ~280 for on-scalp MEG'.
bibliographic_issues: NeuroImage 245:118747 confirmed. arXiv 1912.05401 is by the same six authors (Dec 2019) but carries the earlier title 'Sampling theory for spatial field sensing: Application to electro- and magnetoencephalography'.

checked_sources: Azevedo et al. 2009 (abstract via Europe PMC REST; full text not in PMC)
quote: the adult male human brain contains on average 86.1 +/- 8.1 billion NeuN-positive cells ("neurons")
discrepancy: Numbers match (86.1 +/- 8.1 billion; 'With only 19% of all neurons located in the cerebral cortex'; 0.19 x 86.1 = 16.4 billion, the 'about 16 billion' is derived). Minor nuance: the sample was adult male brains (n = 4), and 'neurons' means NeuN-positive cells.
